blocks.text: A radioactive isotope behaves in just the same way as the normal isotope inside a living organism, but its location and concentration can be found easily by measuring the radiation it emits. So a radioactive isotope acts as an indicator, or tracer, that makes it possible to follow the course of a chemical or biological process. The technique is to substitute radioactive atoms for stable atoms of the same kind in a substance and then follow the 'tagged' atoms with a radiation detector. For example, some chemicals such as hydrogen and sodium in water and food are spread evenly through the body, while others are selectively absorbed by certain organs.

blocks.alt: Composition of Matter: a molecule (about 10^-9 m) contains atoms (10^-10 m); an atom contains a nucleus (10^-15 to 10^-14 m); a nucleus contains neutrons and protons (10^-15 m); a neutron or proton contains quarks (less than 10^-18 m). Curved arrows lead from each level to the next.

blocks.title: Medical tracer
blocks.text: A medical tracer is a substance containing radioactive nuclei that can be introduced into the body and is then absorbed by the tissue being studied, so that its path can be followed from outside the body.

Radioisotopes of many elements can be made easily by bombardment with neutrons and other particles, and as they have become cheap their use in medicine, agriculture, research and industry has grown enormously. They are used to find out how complex chemical reactions proceed, and in biology they have helped to investigate reactions in plants and animals. By mixing a small amount of radioactive isotope with fertiliser, the uptake of fertiliser by a plant can be measured with a radiation detector, so farmers can know the right amount to use. Radiation-induced mutations have produced improved varieties of rice, chickpea, wheat and cotton, with better plant structure, more resistance to diseases and pests, and better yield and grain quality.
Use in medical diagnosis and treatment

Tracers are widely used in medicine to study digestion and the way substances move about in the body. Radio-iodine is absorbed mostly by the thyroid gland, phosphorus by bones and cobalt by the liver, so they can serve as tracers. A small quantity of low-activity radioisotope, mixed with the stable isotope, is given to a patient by injection or otherwise, and its location in diseased tissue is found with radiation detectors. For example, radioactive iodine can show whether the thyroid gland is working properly: a diseased or overactive gland absorbs more than twice the normal amount. Iodine-131 is also used to treat thyroid cancer, and sodium-24 can be used to study the circulation of blood.

Cells that multiply rapidly, such as cancer cells, absorb more radiation and are more easily destroyed by ionising radiation than normal cells. Radioactive tracers in imaging devices have helped in understanding, diagnosing and treating many diseases. Sometimes radioactive capsules called 'seeds' are implanted in malignant tissue for local, short-range treatment; for skin cancer, phosphorus-32 or strontium-90 may be used, but the dose must be carefully controlled to protect healthy tissue. Patients undergoing radiation treatment often feel ill, because the radiation also damages some healthy tissue.
